subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: First, you learn what a network is — devices joined together to share and communicate — and that devices can connect with wires (wired) or without wires (wireless). Second, you learn to spot the many networks around us, and to name the devices on a home network and a school network. Third, you learn about the services on a network — the things you can do, like sharing files, sharing a printer, sending messages, and reaching the web. Fourth, they talk about the good things and the tricky things about networks (advantages and disadvantages). Fifth, they take a gentle first look at staying safe online.

outcomes: Say what a network is — devices joined together so they can share and communicate.
Know that devices connect with wires (wired) or without wires (wireless).
Name some devices found on a home network and a school network.
Describe services on a network — things you can do, such as sharing files, sharing a printer, communicating, and reaching the web.
Talk about one advantage (good thing) and one disadvantage (tricky thing) of a network.

concepts.title: What is a network? Connect and share
concepts.explanation:
A network is two or more devices joined together so they can share things and send messages to each other. Devices can be joined in two ways: with wires (we call this wired) or through the air with no wires (we call this wireless, or Wi-Fi).

At Ehel Academy, all the tablets can use the same printer, and the teacher can send your work to the screen at the front. The tablets, the printer and the screen are joined together. When devices are joined so they can share and talk to each other, we call that a network.
concepts.example: Answer this in your own words, out loud or on paper: What is a network? Connect and share? Then check your answer against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you tell the difference between a wired connection (a cable you can see) and a wireless one (through the air)?

concepts.title: Networks around us
concepts.explanation: Networks are everywhere — in homes, schools, hospitals, shops and offices. The devices on a network depend on what the people need, so a home network and a school network do not have exactly the same devices. In the classroom there are tablets and laptops. In the office there is a printer and a scanner — or one multifunction machine that does printing, scanning and copying all in one. On the wall there is an interactive smartboard, and a projector to show pictures big. All of these are joined on the school network.
concepts.example: At home you might have a laptop, a tablet, smartphones, an e-reader for books, a games console, or a security camera by the door. Some homes even have smart devices like a smart light or a smart fridge that join the home network too.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you notice that networks are found in many different places, not just at school? Can you name two or three devices on a home network and on a school network?

concepts.title: What can we do on a network? (services)
concepts.explanation: The things we can do on a network are called services. The four main services are: sharing files (like photos and work), sharing a printer, communicating (sending messages and emails), and reaching the World Wide Web (the pages on the internet). Maya saves her drawing on the network. Now Nora can open the very same drawing on a different tablet — that is sharing files. The whole class sends your work to one printer in the office — that is sharing a printer.
concepts.example: The teacher sends a message to your parents — that is communicating. And when you look up facts about animals on a web page, you are using the World Wide Web.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you put the steps of a message travelling across the network in a sensible order (type it, it travels, it arrives, it is read)? Can you name at least two services?

concepts.title: Good things and tricky things about networks
concepts.explanation: Networks have good things (we call these advantages) and tricky things (we call these disadvantages). Both are true at the same time — a network is very useful, and it also needs looking after. Sharing is the big one. If the whole class shares one printer, that is cheaper than buying one for every tablet — so sharing saves money. You can share your work with a friend in a second.
concepts.example: You can work together even from different rooms. And your work is kept safely in one place, so it is easy to make a backup — an extra copy — in case anything is lost.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that a network can be very useful and still need looking after? Can you give one advantage and one disadvantage in your own words?

concepts.title: Staying safe online
concepts.explanation: Networks let us share and talk with people who are far away — that is wonderful. Staying safe online is a bit like crossing the road. Crossing the road is fine — we just look after ourselves, and a trusted grown-up helps us. Check yourself: Can you name at least one piece of personal information to keep private?
concepts.example: Online is the same. These are private — we do not give you to people or games we do not know.

esafety.title: Keep personal information private
esafety.text: Your full name, address, school, phone number, birthday and passwords are personal information. Never type them into a game, an app or a website, and never send them to someone you only know online.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

I can know that devices connect with wires (wired) or without wires (wireless).
I can name some devices found on a home network and a school network.
I can describe services on a network — things you can do, such as sharing files, sharing a printer, communicating, and reaching the web.
I can talk about one advantage (good thing) and one disadvantage (tricky thing) of a network.
